::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Purpose"}
Use this guide with the Week 3 readings and class activities. Your completed
notes should help you choose a visualization that matches the analytical
question and explain the design choices that make it easier to interpret.
:::

## Objectives

- match common analytical questions to appropriate chart types;
- distinguish comparison, composition, distribution, time, and relationship
  views;
- evaluate visual encodings, ordering, color, labels, and clutter;
- identify misleading or unnecessary design choices; and
- justify a visualization for a specific audience and purpose.

## Resources

- [Week 3 slides](week_03.qmd)
- [Interpreting Data Visualizations](readings/advanced-interpretation.qmd)
- the assigned Week 3 readings and graph-choice resources in Canvas

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Expectations"}
This work is graded for thoughtful completion. Write enough to show why a chart
or design choice fits the question; a chart name by itself is incomplete.
:::

## 4) Match the question to the chart

Complete the missing chart choices and notes. More than one chart may be
defensible, but your choice must match the variables and comparison.

| Message or question | Chart choice | Data and design notes |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency distribution of categories |  | Use counts or percentages; order categories intentionally. |
| Ranking or nominal comparison |  | Use at least one categorical variable and a count or quantitative summary. |
| Part-to-whole |  | Define one whole; percentages must total 100%. |
| Distribution of one quantitative variable |  | Show shape, center, spread, and unusual values. |
| Change over time |  | Put time on the horizontal axis and preserve chronological order. |
| Relationship between 2 quantitative variables |  | Each mark should represent a meaningful observational unit. |

---

## 5) Justify one choice

Choose a question from a current ECO 230 dataset. In 4-6 sentences:

1. state the question and intended audience;
2. name the variables and their measurement types;
3. select a chart and explain why its visual encoding fits the comparison;
4. identify 2 design decisions you would apply; and
5. name one limitation the visualization would not resolve.
